strengths: The virtual-correspondence construction is an original, practically useful way to obtain approximate hypotheses for difficult three-view problems using existing 5-point/6-point and P3P solvers. The training-free mean-point variant offers a particularly simple implementation. This contribution supports weak acceptance despite the qualifications below.

The experiments demonstrate competitive performance. In Table 1, 4p3v(M±0.15) improves Sacre Coeur AUC@10° from 50.61 for the homotopy-continuation baseline to 52.27. On KITTI, it achieves AUC@5° of 72.05 versus 71.73 for 6pt+P3P, with reported RANSAC runtime decreasing from 0.11 to 0.07 seconds.

The evaluation includes 10,000 real image triplets, controlled noise and outlier experiments, oracle comparisons, and shift-parameter ablations. Figure 3 supports improved convergence per RANSAC iteration under substantial outlier contamination. The authors also acknowledge that the conventional 5pt+P3P baseline remains preferable in some regimes.

The mean-point heuristic has both geometric motivation and empirical support: supplementary Lemma 1 establishes an epipolar-line intersection property, while Figure 2 evaluates the correspondence choice on synthetic data and 452,500 triplets derived from real data. The supplement also provides useful network architecture and training details.
weaknesses: The claimed advantage under limited computation is not fully established. Figure 3 compares iteration counts, although the shifted variants generate multiple hypotheses per iteration and have substantially different costs: Table 1 reports 218.71 microseconds for the shifted mean solver versus 77.90 for 5pt+P3P. Comparisons at equal elapsed time are needed to substantiate this particular claim. Table 1 also shows that 5pt+P3P achieves higher AUC at every reported threshold on both scenes, so the state-of-the-art claim must remain specific to four-correspondence methods.

The evaluation does not measure all unknowns central to the proposed problems. The 4p3vf experiments report pose errors but no focal-length errors. Furthermore, the three-view pose metric evaluates rotation and translation-direction errors for pairs 1–2 and 1–3, leaving the relative scale between their translations untested. These results therefore do not fully validate shared-focal recovery or the complete metric three-camera reconstruction.

The approximation has substantial intrinsic bias: Figure 6 shows appreciable pose errors even with noiseless correspondences. Lemma 1 bounds an image-space distance by triangle size, rather than providing a useful bound on pose error. Although the paper acknowledges this limitation, it does not characterize failure rates by baseline, viewing obliquity, or point geometry, leaving the method's reliable operating range uncertain.

The learned variants add limited demonstrated value relative to their computational cost. For example, Table 1 improves Sacre Coeur AUC@5° only from 44.51 for the shifted mean solver to 44.89 for the shifted learned solver, while per-call runtime increases from 218.71 to 511.28 microseconds. Improvements are inconsistent on KITTI, where the network trained for the calibrated setting is reused.

There are correctable specification and reproducibility issues. Equation (2), as written, is a signed normalized epipolar residual; minimizing it does not minimize Sampson error, and the denominator does not specify restriction to the first two homogeneous components. The implemented loss therefore remains ambiguous. RANSAC thresholds, stopping settings, and local-refinement details are also insufficiently specified, despite their importance to the reported accuracy and runtime.
